name: Milady Décolleté Gillette

image.caption: Vintage Advert for the Milady Decollete Gillette Razor - 1916 (5248628800)

lead: The Milady Décolleté was a razor Gillette introduced in 1915 and advertised as the first safety razor marketed exclusively to women. Its purpose was to remove underarm hair so that women could look smooth in sleeveless and low-cut dresses.

It was largely the company's men's razor with a smaller blade head and special packaging. Advertisements ran in women's magazines and showed women in the latest gowns, and historians credit this marketing with making women a profitable razor market.

paras: It used the same kind of safety razor blade as Gillette's men's models, held in a smaller head, and was sold in a presentation case. Ads presented shaving underarms as part of good grooming.
The product is historical. Modern razor use carries ordinary risks of nicks and irritation.

web.title: The Hair-Raising History of Women's Body Hair - The Henry Ford

angle.text: The razor was sold for removing underarm hair so that bare arms and low necklines looked smooth and groomed, the look the advertisements promoted.

lead: The Milady Décolleté Gillette was a safety razor promoted in 1915-16 as the first marketed exclusively for women.[1]

According to The Henry Ford, it was not specifically designed for women: it was Gillette's men's razor with a smaller blade head and specialised packaging.[2] Gillette, founded in 1901 by King Camp Gillette and renamed in 1904, had begun selling its disposable-blade razor in 1903.[1]

Its advertisements appeared in women's magazines alongside the first underarm hair-removal ads and pictured women in fashionable gowns to show off smooth underarms. The Henry Ford says the campaign worked and made women a profitable market for safety razors.[2]
infobox: Men's razor with smaller head and special packaging[2]

paras: Gillette's company was founded on 28 September 1901 and renamed the Gillette Safety Razor Company in 1904, after the razor began selling in 1903.[1] A 1915-16 advertisement called the Milady Décolleté the first safety razor marketed exclusively to women.[1]
Sources differ on advertisement dates and details; commentators also frame the marketing differently. The Henry Ford article presents it as a successful commercial campaign.[2]
Advertising tied smooth underarms to fashion, showing women in current gowns, in magazines that also carried early hair-removal ads.[2]
